SPRT.01.note: StatsBomb explains expected goals as a probabilistic model trained on historical shots and makes clear that values vary because models use different features and data quality.

article.title: What is xG? How is it calculated?

exercise.prompt: Build a simple shot table with distance, angle, body part, assist type and outcome, then estimate which variables should raise or lower scoring probability and why.

SPRT.02.note: SABR's research guide defines sabermetrics as the search for objective knowledge about baseball and shows how questions, data quality and context matter beyond the Moneyball story.

exercise.prompt: Choose one traditional baseball statistic and design a context-adjusted alternative, stating the decision it should improve and the biases it still cannot remove.

SPRT.03.note: British Cycling's retrospective documents Brailsford's one-percent framing while placing it among coaching, talent, technology, sport science and organizational changes rather than attributing success to tiny tweaks alone.

article.title: Sir Dave Brailsford at British Cycling — A Career Retrospective

exercise.prompt: Break one performance goal into ten contributing systems, estimate the likely effect and measurement cost of improving each, and reject changes whose claimed gains cannot be tested.

SPRT.04.note: The consensus statement defines internal and external training load, explains why monitoring is useful, and emphasizes individual context instead of universal workload thresholds.

article.title: Monitoring Athlete Training Loads: Consensus Statement
article.source: International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance — PubMed

exercise.prompt: Plan a four-week training block with objective external load, subjective internal load, recovery markers, progression, deloading and rules for changing the plan when responses differ.

SPRT.05.note: Joyner and Coyle frame elite endurance through the interaction of maximal oxygen uptake, lactate threshold and movement economy rather than treating any one number as destiny.

article.title: Endurance Exercise Performance: The Physiology of Champions
article.source: M. J. Joyner and E. F. Coyle — PubMed

exercise.prompt: Compare two hypothetical runners with different VO2 max, fractional threshold and running economy, then explain why the athlete with the larger VO2 max need not be faster.

SPRT.06.note: The official Court judgment records how transfer fees after contract expiry and nationality quotas conflicted with EU freedom-of-movement law for workers.

article.title: Judgment of the Court of 15 December 1995 — Bosman, Case C-415/93
article.source: Court of Justice of the European Union — EUR-Lex

exercise.prompt: Trace the pre-Bosman and post-Bosman career path of an out-of-contract EU player, separating employment mobility, transfer compensation, squad quotas and later market consequences.

SPRT.07.note: FIFA's Training Centre analyses contemporary principles such as blocks, third-player combinations and counter-pressing while showing tactics as coordinated behaviours, not just formation diagrams.

exercise.prompt: Analyse one match in possession, transition and out of possession, recording shape, pressing triggers, rest defence, overloads, rotations and adaptations to the opponent.

SPRT.08.note: The paper exposes the probabilistic assumptions beneath Elo, including expected scores, update sensitivity and the special difficulty of modelling draws and team sports.

article.title: Understanding and Pushing the Limits of the Elo Rating Algorithm
article.source: Leszek Szczecinski and Aymen Djebbi — arXiv

exercise.prompt: Implement Elo updates for four players, vary the K-factor and expected-score scale, and show how upset results, inactivity, draws and new entrants affect ratings.

SPRT.09.note: The German ghost-game study uses COVID-era empty stadiums as a natural experiment and finds that crowd effects vary by league rather than explaining all of home advantage.

article.title: Does Crowd Support Drive the Home Advantage in Professional Football? Evidence from German Ghost Games during the COVID-19 Pandemic
article.source: Kai Fischer and Justus Haucap — Journal of Sports Economics

exercise.prompt: Design a home-advantage model with travel, familiarity, crowd, referee decisions, team strength and schedule, then explain why before-after empty-stadium comparisons can still be confounded.

SPRT.10.note: The university module introduces linear and angular kinematics, kinetics, force plates and motion analysis as tools for explaining movement rather than merely judging how technique looks.

article.title: Introduction to Sport and Exercise Biomechanics

exercise.prompt: Record a jump or throw in slow motion, estimate joint angles and centre-of-mass motion, and draw the external forces and moments that produce the movement.

SPRT.11.note: WADA's current operating guidelines explain longitudinal biological monitoring, adaptive limits, expert review, sample requirements and how the passport complements direct substance detection.

exercise.prompt: Create a fictional longitudinal blood profile, add plausible altitude, illness and doping scenarios, and describe why expert review and chain-of-custody evidence are needed before sanction.

SPRT.12.note: The systematic review found widespread high risk of bias, weak reporting, overfitting and little external validation, so current models should not be treated as dependable individual injury forecasts.

article.title: Just How Confident Can We Be in Predicting Sports Injuries? A Systematic Review of Existing Musculoskeletal Injury Prediction Models in Sport
article.source: Garrett S. Bullock et al. — Sports Medicine / PubMed

exercise.prompt: Audit an injury model for leakage, class imbalance, calibration, missing data, overfitting, external validation and decision usefulness, then distinguish prediction from preventable cause.
